source.title: Augmentation Strategies for Learning with Noisy Labels
source.authors: Kento Nishi; Yi Ding; Alex Rich; Tobias Höllerer

record.file_problem: The full text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study examines how augmentation changes the clean-versus-noisy loss behavior that noisy-label methods rely on, and reports that strong augmentation can disrupt that behavior.
record.gate_note: The study reports many classification-accuracy comparisons for augmentation methods, but those do not measure the claim versions' named outcomes. Figure 2 and its accompanying text report a result about clean-versus-noisy loss distributions during warm-up.
record.test_reason: Section 4.3 and Figure 2 directly examine clean versus noisy training-sample losses under different augmentation strengths. The authors report that excessive early augmentation disrupts the loss separation associated with V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the relevant conclusion: excessive augmentation during warm-up can impair clean-before-noisy learning, especially at high noise rates. The broader conclusion is that weak augmentation for loss analysis and strong augmentation for gradient updates improve noisy-label classification performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies augmentation strategies in noisy-label training and measures loss behavior; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The clean-versus-noisy loss behavior during warm-up changes with the chance of applying strong augmentation; the authors also report downstream accuracy differences across noise levels and warm-up augmentation choices, but those accuracy results do not directly measure a claim version.
record.problems: The relevant loss-distribution result is described without numeric values or uncertainty estimates; the text gives a qualitative interpretation of Figure 2. The study does not test random labels or report training error for the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: Classification accuracy comparisons in Tables 1–6 are not rows because they do not measure the outcomes named by the claim versions. Table 2 compares downstream accuracy under warm-up augmentation choices; Figure 2 provides the directly relevant loss-distribution result recorded in R1.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting without architecture or hyperparameter changes.
Relative training time for true versus random labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout a corruption sweep and steadily increasing test error toward chance. Noise-robust method accuracy comparisons do not establish this joint behavior.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing regularization preserves true-label generalization.
The full temporal sequence of shared-pattern learning followed by noise memorization, eventual noisy-label fitting, and behavior with completely random labels.

record.verdict_notes: Figure 2 provides a qualitative snapshot at epoch 20, not training trajectories or numerical evidence of reversed loss ordering. Tables 1–6 report downstream method performance and do not independently justify verdicts on the claim versions.

versions.untested_parts: No experiment tests completely random labels, training error, or test error at chance.
Training time and convergence speed as label corruption increases are not reported.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs are tested.
The study reports test accuracy at several synthetic noise levels, but does not report perfect training fit or a smooth rise in test error toward chance.
The study does not test whether weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation prevent random-label fitting, or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.

The study examines clean versus noisy label loss behavior under augmentation during warm-up, but does not test completely random labels or establish the full training-time sequence of fitting shared patterns before memorizing noise.

rows.subject: 18-layer PreAct Resnet
rows.operation_detail: Measured normalized loss distributions for clean and noisy training-set segments while varying the chance of strong augmentation during warm-up.

conditions.value: stochastically applied strong augmentation with increasing chance

rows.measure: Normalized loss distribution for samples associated with clean versus noisy dataset segments
rows.value: Applying too much augmentation too soon can encourage clean-segment samples to have higher loss and noisy-segment samples to have lower loss.
rows.note: The text describes the direction of the distribution change but gives no numeric values; the figure is described as showing the distributions. The result qualifies the clean-before-noisy behavior under strong augmentation rather than testing the full V6 sequence.
rows.check: The qualitative result supports impaired clean-versus-noisy loss separation, but does not establish reversed ordering or the complete learning sequence. The baseline should identify the lower-probability strong-augmentation conditions in Figure 2. Exact augmentation probabilities and distribution values are unavailable in the supplied text. Epoch 20 is stated, although the default CIFAR-10 warm-up lasts 10 epochs; the experiment's warm-up duration is unclear.

source_check.correct: The text confirms 90% label noise, epoch 20, and varying strong-augmentation probability; it does not identify the dataset for Figure 2. No numerical baseline is stated.

relationships.condition: PreAct ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 with 90% label noise, with strong augmentation applied frequently during early training
relationships.reason: R1 reports higher clean-sample losses and lower noisy-sample losses with excessive early augmentation, weakening the early loss separation associated with clean-first learning; it does not establish a full reversal.
relationships.display_finding: Clean-sample losses increased while noisy-sample losses decreased, weakening early loss separation without establishing a reversal of learning order.
